deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. The page has no derivation. It is one month (März) of a precomputed table. Each row holds the quantities needed to reduce mean star places to apparent places (aberration plus the solar part of nutation). They are the quantities later standardised as Bessel's day numbers A, B, C, D and the 'independent' numbers h, H, i. The Feb and April pages continue the same table. Feb row 29 equals März row 1, and März row 32 equals April row 1.

COLUMNS, identified by recomputation (the identifications are mine; Gauss gives no headings):

(1) τ, the elapsed fraction of the year. It grows by 0.002730 per row: (0.3337 − 0.0907)/89 = 0.0027303. This equals 0.99727/365.25. So successive rows are one sidereal day apart, i.e. successive culminations of a star, not civil days. τ = 0 falls about 1 day before Jan 0. The header '60 + r' (and '91 +' on the April page) seems to be the day count from Jan 0.

(2) A = τ − 0.0200·sin 2☉. Checks: col2 − col1 = +0.0199 at ☉ = 313.7°, +0.0029 at 355.8°, −0.0158 at 26.3°. This is τ plus the solar nutation in longitude divided by the annual precession. It implies Δψ_solar ≈ −1.00″ sin 2☉ (taking precession ≈ 50.2″). The lunar (node) terms are absent, so this is a year-independent 'solar' table.

(3) B = −0.434·cos 2☉ (arcsec): the solar nutation in obliquity. The coefficient is pinned to 0.433–0.435 by the rounding of rows 7–14. The ratio 0.434/1.00 is about tan ε, as in the classical solar nutation ratio.

(4) ☉, the Sun's true longitude in ° ′ ″ at each row. The equinox (☉ = 0) falls between rows 19 and 20 of March. The daily step falls from 60′39″ (Feb 1) to 57′48″ (end of April). That is the true solar motion times 0.99727, consistent with sidereal-day spacing.

(5) i = C·tan ε = −κ sin ε cos ☉. Ratio col5/col6 = 0.4342 = tan 23°28′. The coincidence with log₁₀e is accidental.

(6) C = −κ cos ε cos ☉.

(7) D = −κ sin ☉.

From (6) and (7), κ ≈ 20.60–20.61″ and κ cos ε ≈ 18.91″.

(8) H and (9) log h, defined by h sin H = C and h cos H = D (H in degrees.minutes).
- Mar 1: h = √(17.97² + 6.41²) = 19.08, log = 1.2805; H = 289°38–39′.
- Mar 20: H ≈ 270° when D ≈ 0; log h = log(κ cos ε) = 1.2766.

The point of h, H is that the aberration in right ascension, C cos α + D sin α, collapses to h·sin(H + α). The declination term then involves h·cos(H + α)·sin δ plus i·cos δ. These allow one-line log computation per star.

Recomputed spot checks:
- Row 8: C = −18.55, D = 3.99, H = 282°08′, log h = 1.2782 (table 1.2781).
- Row 21: H = 268°06′ (written '268 6').
- Row 7: H = 283°12′.
- Row 18: D = +0.44.

The table is internally consistent to the last unit.
errors: No substantive errors found; the table recomputes to within last-digit rounding.
Row 25, column C: recomputation gives −18.82 (−18.909·cos 5.686°); the blotted last digit may be 1 or 2. This is borderline rounding.
Row 7, column B: −0.40 requires a coefficient ≥ 0.4333. This is consistent with the other rows (c ≈ 0.434), so it is not an error.

Aberration constant implied ≈ 20.6″, larger than the contemporary standard values (Delambre/Bessel ≈ 20.25″, Struve 20.445″). This is a choice of constant, not a computational slip; noted as uncertain/peculiar.

results.what: Tabulation of reduction quantities τ, A (solar part), B (solar part), C, D for star reductions, at sidereal-day intervals
results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers A, B, C, D
results.usually_credited_to: F. W. Bessel (Fundamenta Astronomiae 1818; Tabulae Regiomontanae 1830)

results.what: Auxiliary quantities h, H with h sin H = C, h cos H = D, and i = C tan ε, tabulated as log h, H, i
results.modern_name: Bessel's independent day numbers h, H, i (auxiliary-angle form of the aberration reduction)

results.what: Solar nutation terms Δψ ≈ −1.00″ sin 2☉, Δε ≈ 0.434″ cos 2☉ folded into A and B

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational ephemeris table for reducing star places (aberration and solar nutation in the Bessel day-number form with h, H, i). It is consistent with Gauss's well-known observatory work. Its only mild interest is that it uses sidereal-day spacing and an aberration constant of about 20.6″. Dating it relative to Bessel's 1830 publication might be of minor historical interest.
